column12: On August 26, 2025, the Arkansas Public Service Commission approved Arkansas Electric Cooperative Corporation (AECC)'s new Transmission Extension of Facilities Tariff (TEOF), as originally filed in May, 2025. AECC designed TEOF as a mechanism to recover costs of anticipated required transmission upgrades and extensions to serve the rising number and unique nature of new interconnection requests that several of its 17 member cooperatives have received from "power-intensive users" (PIUs). Customers requesting service under this tariff would enter into a service agreement with an AECC member cooperative or be subject to a member cooperative's tariffs within the allocated service territory where the interconnection will occur. Some AECC member cooperatives may need to develop their own tariffs to pass through benefits and expenses to the PIU. AECC defines an PIU as a retail customer with a demand exceeding 50 MW, either as a single user or aggregated load. Under the TEOF, AECC would collect transmission costs from relevant member cooperatives, which could collect the cost from PIUs. The tariff is designed to capture and directly assign additional transmission expenses to PIUs while maintaining reliability and affordability for all member cooperatives and end-users. AECC noted that PIU customers seek higher-voltage interconnection than AECC's typical investments for average-load customers, making PIU costs higher (e.g., as high as $7 million / line mile) than average (e.g., $2 million / line mile).  Provisions include Contribution In Aid of Construction and a proposed Transmission Reimbursement Agreement to facilitate payments.

On March 10, 2026, the Arkansas Public Service Commission approved Southwest Arkansas Electric Cooperative Coorporation's new Industrial Power rate for industrial customers up to 50 MW requiring transformer capacity over 10,000 kVA. The rate includes a monthly customer charge, a demand charge based on measured peak demand, and an energy charge. The minimum bill is the customer charge. Billing demand is based on either 1) the maximum kW demand during any 15-minute interval in the billing period or 2) 90% of the maximum measured demand established during the previous 12 months; there would also be a 98% minimum power factor, in line with the Cooperative's existing power factors.

The application notes that the tariff is beholden to the Cooperative's existing Extension of Facilities Policy. This includes finacial security via a surety bond, irrevocable letter of credit, parent guaranty, or other acceptable mechanism. It also includes a facilities charge to recover costs not collected through Contribution-In-Aid-Of-Construction.

In March 2025, as part of a general rate case, SWEPCO proposed revisions to one of the options included in its economic development rider. Under the proposal, SWEPCO would no longer list "server farms and information technology-related companies" as an example of businesses and industries eligible for service under Option 2, which is available for customers receiving service under the Lighting and Power rate schedule and bringing new loads of 200 kW or more. The proposal does not include changes for Option 1, which is available for new loads of 500kW or more, or significant expansions of existing load in excess of 500kW incremental load, or for resumption of service to loads of a minimum of 500kW which have been inactive for 12 months or more, and take service under the Lighting and Power rate or the Large Lighting and Power rate (10,000 kW or greater). The availability of Option 1 is at the sole discretion of the utility; SWEPCO will not accept new applications for service under Option 1 when its forecasts indicate that additional generating capacity will be needed within a three-year period. SWEPCO filed a settlement agreement on November 7, 2025, which did not mention the proposed changes, only amending filing deadlines under the rider. On January 23, 2026, the Arkansas Public Service Commission filed an order approving the settlement agreement in full. SWEPCO's compliance tariffs did include the originally proposed changes, removing mention of server farms and information technology-related companies and clarifying that Option 1 is at its sole discretion; the compliance tariffs also integrated the filing deadlines from the settlement.

On November 25, 2025, Black Hills Energy proposed a new economic development tariff for Large Power Service customers who 1) will add at least 3 MW of load in a new or existing location in the utility's territory and 2) demonstrate that the cost of electricity is a critical consideration in deciding where to locate a facility. The 3 MW minimum is based on the maximum 15-minute integrated measured demand during a billing period; the minimum bill is based on 3 MW. For each MW of minimum load over 40 MW, the customer would be billed at the standard rate. The rider would offer a 30% discount to base rate energy and demand charges and would be exempt from certain adjustment riders. The standard contract term is 10 years; contract terms 10-25 years would require regulatory approval. Loads up to 40 MW would not require regulatory approval; loads over 40 MW would require regulatory approval. Customers must fund any necessary T&D extensions under the utility's line extension policies and any generation asset acquired specifically to serve the customer; Black Hills is also amending its line extension policies to exclude Economic Development Rate customers from allowances.

Black Hills filed a settlement agreement on February 19, 2026, which would approve the tariff with modifications. The tariff would be limited to 100 MW, at which point Black Hills must request a regulatory variance; the cap would reset when Black Hills updates its marginal capacity costs. Participants would receive the 30% discount and be exempt from the Transmission Cost Adjustment rider, but must still pay the Demand Side Management Cost Adjustment, Renewable Energy Standard Adjustment, and Clean Energy Plan Rider. Participants must perform at least one system benefit activity: maintain a load factor above system average, maintain a favorable load shape, subscribe to the interruptible load tariff, install behind-the-meter renewable energy or storage, install demand-side management measures, contribute to a low-income program, install electric vehicle charging, obtain LEED certification, or implement a customer-designed measure that provides system benefits. Customers not enrolled in the tariff would be held harmless and not responsible for any costs incurred on behalf of participants.

On February 28, 2025, as part of its 2025 general rate case filing with the Florida Public Service Commission, Florida Power and Light Company (FPL) proposed two new rate schedules, Large Load Contract Service One (LLCS-1) and Large Load Contract Service Two (LLCS-2), to support the integration of substantial new customer loads. LLCS-1 is capped at 3,000 MW and available only in three designated zones near Sunbreak in St. Lucie County, Tesoro in Martin County, and Sugar in Palm Beach County, areas chosen for their proximity to FPL’s 500 kilovolt transmission infrastructure and suitability for new generation. The schedule includes a stated rate for incremental generation capacity, which will be updated in future rate proceedings, and will close to new load once the 3,000 megawatt limit is reached. LLCS-2 offers similar service to customers outside the LLCS-1 zones but does not include a megawatt cap or a fixed rate for incremental generation; instead, charges will vary based on the specific infrastructure needed to serve each customer’s load, offering geographic flexibility in exchange for cost variability. 

On August 20, 2025, FPL and other stakeholders filed a joint stipulation and settlement agreement. If approved, the agreement would take effect on January 1, 2026, and remain in place through December 31, 2029, or until new base rates are established. The proposed settlement includes approval of LLCS-1 and LLCS-2, with key modifications including a higher minimum load (50 MW), reduced minimum take-or-pay demand charge (70%), revisions to financial assurance requirements, and other proposed changes. The settlement agreement was approved by the Commission on November 20, 2025.

column3: Rule 13 (R13): Line Extensions-- Capacity Reservation Charge and Excess Demand Charge
column12:
Pacific Power updated several of its line extension conditions and definitions as part of a general rate case filed February 14, 2024 and approved by the Oregon Public Utility Commission on February 24, 2025. This includes two charges that apply to very large customers beginning July 1, 2025.

The Capacity Reservation Charge (Rule 13, Sheet R13-1) ensures adequate cost recovery from customers using less power than they reserved. It is a per-kW charge that Pacific Power may apply to monthly bills for excess reserved capacity, allowing for a 10% buffer. This charge applies to customers with total expected loads exceeding 50,000 kW. It is designed to recover the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC) transmission function revenue requirements to meet the customer's anticipated peak demand, plus a percentage of fixed generation costs reflecting the utility's costs to meet planning reserve margins incorporating the customer's forecast peak load.

The Excess Demand Charge (Rule 13, Sheet R13-2) is a mechanism to recover costs of any unexpected market purchases needed to meet customer demand beyond what was reserved. It is a per-kW charge that Pacific Power may apply when a customer's total load exceeds forecasts stipulated in written agreements. It is designed to ensure that customers do not underestimate their needed load and operate their facilities within the bounds of their load request.

This rate is designed to attract new large and high-load-factor customer loads that provide net benefits to the utility's customers and communities. As part of a general rate case filed on November 14, 2025, Texas-New Mexico Power proposed a new Primary Service Substation rate class, carved out from the existing Primary Interval Data Recording (IDR) rate. The IDR rate is for customers connected to primary distribution, all of whom have the same delivery rate. The rate allows customers who design, build, and maintain their own distribution infrastructure — typically large industrial users like oil and gas producers and data centers — to receive a lower rate than other primary IDR customers, since their self-sufficient buildouts reduce dependence on TNMP's broader distribution system. Separation of this rate class from the existing primary IDR rate would affect approximately nine existing customers.

column3: Electric Service Regulation No. 12: Line Extensions
column12:
In RMP’s general rate case (Docket No. 24-035-04), initially filed in June 2024 and amended in August, the company proposed introducing two new charges for large line extensions: a Capacity Reservation Charge (CRC) and an Excess Damage Charge (EDC). These charges were intended to address discrepancies between reserved and actual usage, as well as usage exceeding contracted amounts. RMP also proposed treating certain line extensions as speculative or requiring special contracts, suggesting that some projects could be denied service. In addition, the utility proposed classifying line extension facilities as either network upgrades or direct-assigned facilities, affecting cost allocation between the utility and its customers.

A settlement filed on January 14, 2025, eliminated the proposed CRC and EDC. In their place, modifications were made to the existing monthly On-Peak Power Charge and a new Excess Power Charge was introduced. These changes apply to large customers with significant reserved capacity and are designed to better align charges with actual demand. The settlement was approved by the Commission in an order issued on April 25, 2025.

Separately, in August 2024, the Utah Division of Public Utilities requested that the Public Service Commission open a docket (24-035-43) to investigate and solicit public comment on Rocky Mountain Power’s (RMP) Electric Service Regulation No. 12 (Line Extensions). The request was prompted by numerous complaints regarding the limitations, delays, and costs associated with the utility’s current line extension practices for large new loads. In August 2025, the Commission stated that it will take no further action until its rulemaking proceeding, 25-R318-01, is complete.

In December 2024, Virginia's State Corporation Commission approved Dominion Energy's application to create a voluntary, experimental tariff to support carbon-free and renewable energy generation for its non-residential customers. The Carbon-Free or Renewable Generation Supply Service (Schedule CFG) allows non-residential customers to purchase the net energy output from carbon-free or renewable energy resources and their environmental attributes in an amount up to 100% of their energy needs. Participating energy facilities must have a nameplate capacity of 1,000 kW or more, and will be sourced either by Dominion Energy itself or through a contract with a third-party. 

No more than 50 customers can elect service under this schedule; after that, the schedule will not be available. Participation is available on a voluntary basis for any customer receiving service on a variety of existting non-residential schedules, including those for small, intermediate, and large customers.

In February 2025, Rappahannock Electric Cooperative (REC) gained approval from the Virginia State Corporation Commission (VA SCC) to form a series of for-profit subsidiaries to help it serve new "exceptionally-sized customers." Under the arrangement, the affiliates will obtain power supply and provide it to REC on a wholesale basis; REC would then deliver it to customers on a retail basis. In March 2025, REC requested approval for a new Schedule LP-DF: Large Power Dedicated Facilities Rate Schedule to structure this service. Schedule LP-DF would be mandatory for all eligible new large, high load factor customers served by multi-tenant (colocation) data centers that lease space to other organizations, as well as other "dedicated distribution facilities." Schedule LP-DF is designed to recover the full cost of obtaining power supply and providing distribution service to these customers, including a delivery service charge and service charge (both on the basis of per-MVA installed), excess facilities charge, and a pass-through of power supply costs. Customers taking service under the tariff would be responsible for any additional facilities needed to prevent interference to transmission or distribution systems. REC states that it designed charges based on forecasts for customers that will begin taking service in the next two years, and that it will monitor the rate and request adjustments if necessary as additional Schedule LP-DF customers come online. 

In April 2025, VA SCC granted REC's request to place Schedule LP-DF into effect on an interim basis, subject to refund, on and after July 1, 2025. Comments and investigations have been ongoing. In August 2025, VA SCC staff filed findings and recommendations for the State Corporation Commission’s consideration; these can be found within the docket link.

There are currently no customers taking service under LPD-1. Schedule LPD-2 will be available to new large load consumers with an expected metered load of 40,000 kW or higher served at a voltage of 20kV or higher through dedicated facilities. LPD-2 is intended to meet large-load customers' distribution and power supply requirements, to recover the full cost of providing such service, and mitigate the financial and operational risks associated with serving large-load consumers. Consumers' costs would reflect market-based rates, including wholesale market prices for power purchases, and all capacity and transmission charges incurred by the cooperative to serve them. New customers that meet LPD-2 eligibility criteria are required to take service under it; accordingly, SVEC also proposed revisions to two other non-residential rate schedules that clarify this. SVEC also filed-- for informational purposes-- corresponding revisions to its Terms and Conditions of Service approved by the SVEC Board of Directors that it intends to implement in conjunction with Schedule LPD-2.

On March 25, 2025, the Public Service Commission approved a stipulation that adopted revisions to Appalachian Power Company’s existing Large Capacity Power (LCP) and Industrial Power (IP) tariffs. The revisions took effect on January 1, 2025 and apply to new load and expansions of existing load that is greater than or equal to 100 MW at an individual site or 150 MW on an aggregated basis. The revisions establish a minimum contract term of 12 years. A large load customer may designate a load ramp period of up to 5 years, after which point the mandatory 12 year period will commence.

Large load customers must provide collateral in a form acceptable to the utility based upon the creditworthiness of the customer. The amount of collateral provided must be equal to 24 times the Large Load Customer’s previous maximum monthly non-fuel bill. Large load customers may reduce their contract capacity at any time after the first 5 years of the Initial Contract Term by up to 20% by giving the utility at least 42 months written notice. Customers may terminate their contract or reduce their contract capacity beyond 20% at any time after the first 5 years of the Initial Contract Term by giving the utility at least 42 months written notice and paying an exit fee.
